Series::CalcAccessor::antidiff¶

Back to Series::CalcAccessor API Reference

Related Accessor Methods¶

x.calc.antidiff is also an accessor with named methods for stochastic integrals along a path: ito, strat, theta, marcus and their running forms. They are documented on their own pages, linked under See Also. The call form on this page is unchanged.

Signatures¶

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::antidiff(Fn&& fn) const

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::antidiff(Fn&& fn, double lower) const

template<class Fn>
Series Series::CalcAccessor::antidiff(
    Fn&& fn,
    double lower,
    const Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions& options) const

What It Computes¶

antidiff() evaluates an anchored integral at every value of the owning Series. For first order, receiver u, lower bound a, and callback g, the result is

F(u) = integral from a to u of g(t) dt + F(a)

The callback is the integrand, not a precomputed sample array. The method chooses quadrature nodes, passes all nodes to fn in one batched Series, and combines the returned values with Simpson or trapezoidal weights. This is the callable counterpart to sampled-data Series::AntidiffAccessor::trapezoid, not an alias for it.

The receiver supplies upper endpoints. A scalar receiver produces a scalar; a vector, matrix, or higher-rank receiver produces one integral per element and keeps its shape. A value below lower is valid: node spacing becomes negative, so the integral has the mathematically correct reversed orientation.

Repeated Integration¶

options.order = n requests the nth anchored antiderivative. The engine uses the weighted identity

F_n(u) = sum(k=0..n-1) F_n^(k)(a) * (u-a)^k / k!
       + integral from a to u of (u-t)^(n-1) * g(t) / (n-1)! dt

rather than recursively nesting n independent quadrature calls. This keeps endpoint lanes batched and evaluates the integrand once per refinement level.

initial[k] is F_n^(k)(lower) for k = 0 .. n-1. An empty initial means all those conditions are zero. Supplying some but not all conditions is an error because it would leave the requested antiderivative under-specified.

Callback Shape Contract¶

If the receiver shape is U and one estimate uses m quadrature nodes, fn receives shape U + [m]. It must return exactly that shape on the same platform. Write the callback entirely with shape-preserving Series operations:

auto g = [](const pluss::Series& t) {
  return t.square().mul((-t).exp());
};

Do not reduce the node axis inside the callback; antidiff() owns that reduction. All returned values must be finite. A singularity sampled on the closed interval is reported instead of allowing NaN or infinity to poison the estimate.

Quadrature And Convergence¶

Rule::Simpson is the default and rounds an odd interval request upward to an even count, with a minimum of two. Rule::Trapezoid accepts any positive interval count. With adaptive=true, the method doubles the interval count until

max(abs(refined - previous)) <= atol + rtol * max(abs(refined))

or max_refinements is exhausted. require_convergence=true turns exhaustion into an error; false returns the last estimate. The error estimate controls quadrature refinement only. It is not a proof that the callback is smooth or that a sampled singularity does not exist between nodes.

Options¶

Field

Meaning

Default

order

Number of anchored integrations

1

lower

Bound used by the no-bound overload

unset

initial

F^(k)(lower) for k=0..order-1

all zero

rule

Rule::Simpson or Rule::Trapezoid

Rule::Simpson

intervals

Starting interval count

256

adaptive

Double intervals until tolerance is met

true

atol

Absolute convergence tolerance

1e-10

rtol

Relative convergence tolerance

1e-8

max_refinements

Maximum interval doublings

8

require_convergence

Throw if refinement exhausts its budget

true

elementwise and strict_dependency belong to differentiation and are ignored here.

Examples¶

Example 1. One vectorized call integrates four upper endpoints and preserves their matrix shape.

auto upper = pluss::make_series({{0.5, 1.0}, {1.5, 2.0}});

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.intervals = 32;
options.adaptive = false;

auto area = upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.square(); },
    0.0,
    options);

std::cout << area << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.041666667, 0.33333333],
  [1.125, 2.6666667]]

Example 2. An upper endpoint below the lower bound reverses orientation. Here integral_0^-1 t dt = 1/2.

auto upper = pluss::make_series(-1.0);
std::cout << upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t; }, 0.0) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=0.5

Example 3. A second antiderivative needs two lower-bound conditions. For F''(u)=1, F(0)=2, and F'(0)=3, the result is F(u)=2+3u+u^2/2.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;
options.initial = {2.0, 3.0};
options.intervals = 32;
options.adaptive = false;

auto upper = pluss::make_series({{0.5, 1.0}, {1.5, 2.0}});
auto result = upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.mul(0.0).add(1.0); },
    0.0,
    options);

std::cout << result << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[3.625, 5.5],
  [7.625, 10]]

Example 4. Empty initial conditions do not infer constants; they explicitly select the zero-anchored member of the antiderivative family.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.order = 2;
options.intervals = 32;
options.adaptive = false;

auto upper = pluss::make_series({{0.5, 1.0}, {1.5, 2.0}});
options.initial.clear();
std::cout << upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.mul(0.0).add(1.0); },
    0.0,
    options) << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.125, 0.5],
  [1.125, 2]]

Example 5. Fixed Simpson and trapezoidal estimates expose the accuracy tradeoff without adaptive refinement. Both use eight intervals for integral_0^1 t^4 dt, whose exact value is 0.2.

using Calc = pluss::Series::CalcAccessor;
auto upper = pluss::make_series(1.0);

Calc::CalcOptions trap;
trap.rule = Calc::Rule::Trapezoid;
trap.intervals = 8;
trap.adaptive = false;

Calc::CalcOptions simpson = trap;
simpson.rule = Calc::Rule::Simpson;

auto fourth = [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.pow(4.0); };
std::cout << std::setprecision(10);
std::cout << "trap=" << upper.calc.antidiff(fourth, 0.0, trap).item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "simpson=" << upper.calc.antidiff(fourth, 0.0, simpson).item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

trap=0.2052001953
simpson=0.2000325521

Example 6. Adaptive Simpson refinement resolves a smooth oscillatory integrand.

auto upper = pluss::make_series(std::numbers::pi);
auto area = upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.sin(); }, 0.0);

std::cout << area.item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

2

Example 7. Binding a lower bound and policy avoids repeating configuration; an explicit lower bound still wins for that call.

pluss::Series::CalcAccessor::CalcOptions options;
options.lower = 0.0;
options.intervals = 32;
options.adaptive = false;

auto upper = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0});
auto configured = upper.calc(options);
auto square = [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.square(); };

std::cout << "bound=" << configured.antidiff(square) << "\n";
std::cout << "override=" << configured.antidiff(square, 1.0) << "\n";

Output¶

bound=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.041666667, 0.33333333, 1.125, 2.6666667]
override=pluss::Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.29166667, 0, 0.79166667, 2.3333333]

Example 8. The upper endpoint remains differentiable. The derivative of an anchored integral with respect to its upper endpoint is the integrand evaluated there.

auto upper = pluss::make_series(0.75);
upper.tracks_slope_(true);

auto area = upper.calc.antidiff(
    [](const pluss::Series& t) { return t.square(); }, 0.0);
area.reverse();

std::cout << "area=" << area.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "darea_dupper=" << upper.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

Output¶

area=0.140625
darea_dupper=0.5625

Empty Inputs¶

An empty real floating receiver returns an empty clone with the same shape, dtype, and platform. No callback evaluation is needed because there are no endpoints.

Failure Modes¶

  • The receiver must be defined and have a real floating dtype.

  • lower must be finite. The no-bound overload requires options.lower.

  • order must be at least one; intervals must be positive.

  • atol and rtol must be finite and non-negative.

  • initial must be empty or contain exactly order values.

  • rule must be Rule::Simpson or Rule::Trapezoid.

  • The callback must return a defined, finite Series with the exact node shape and platform it received.

  • Adaptive exhaustion throws when require_convergence is true.

  • Doubling an interval count that would overflow int64 throws before the multiplication.

Representative diagnostics are stable:

Series.calc.antidiff: no lower bound; pass one or bind it with x.calc({.lower = a})
Series.calc.antidiff: integrand output shape must match the quadrature-node shape
Series.calc.antidiff: initial must be empty or contain one value per order
Series.calc.antidiff: rule is not recognized
